concepts.title: Lorentz Force on a Moving Charge
concepts.definition: A charge travelling through crossed electric and magnetic fields feels one combined push: q times the electric field plus q times the cross product of its velocity with the magnetic field. The magnetic share has size qvB sin(theta) and points sideways to both velocity and field.
concepts.key_idea: Magnetic force vanishes for a resting charge or motion along the field, does no work, and flips sign for negative carriers.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.2.2 (Eq. 4.3, tesla unit definition, Examples 4.1-4.2)

solution_steps.explain: the cross product of velocity and field has magnitude vB sin(theta)

solution_steps.action: scale by the sine of the angle
solution_steps.explain: only the velocity part across the field counts, giving qvB sin(theta)

concepts.title: Force on a Current-Carrying Wire
concepts.definition: A straight conductor of length l carrying current I sitting in an external field B feels a sideways force IlB sin(theta); the length vector points along the current and B must be the imposed field, not the wire's own.
concepts.key_idea: The rod result comes from adding qv x B over every drifting carrier, and curved wires follow by integrating Idl x B.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.2.3 (Eq. 4.4 derivation from drift velocity)
question_patterns: a wire of length l carries current I inside a field B; find the force on it

determine the sideways push on a current-carrying conductor from I, l and B

solution_steps.explain: the current-length product is the source strength in F = Il x B
magnitude is IlB sin(theta) with theta between wire and field

concepts.title: Field That Suspends a Wire Against Gravity
concepts.definition: A current-carrying wire can float in a horizontal magnetic field when the upward magnetic pull exactly cancels its weight; equating IlB with mg yields the balancing field strength.
concepts.key_idea: Mid-air suspension is a force balance: magnetic lift equals weight, so B = mg over Il.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.2.3 (Example 4.1 suspended wire, 0.65 T result)

solution_steps.explain: gravity pulls down with mass times g
setting IlB equal to the weight gives B = mg over Il

concepts.title: Radius of the Circular Orbit in a Magnetic Field
concepts.definition: When a charge crosses a uniform field at right angles, the sideways magnetic force plays the centripetal role, so the particle runs around a circle whose radius grows with momentum and shrinks with charge and field.
concepts.key_idea: Bigger momentum means a wider circle; the field bends the path without changing the speed.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.3 (Eq. 4.5, Example 4.3 electron radius 28 cm)
question_patterns: an electron enters a field of 6e-4 T perpendicular to it at 3e7 m/s; find the circle radius

compute the radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field

determine how the circle radius changes when the momentum doubles

solution_steps.explain: the radius is proportional to the momentum mv
qvB supplies the centripetal force, so r = mv over qB

concepts.title: Cyclotron Frequency
concepts.definition: A charge circling in a uniform field completes revolutions at a rate fixed by qB over 2 pi m; remarkably this frequency ignores how fast the particle moves or how wide its circle is.
concepts.key_idea: Speed-independence of the rotation frequency is exactly what lets a cyclotron keep accelerating particles in step.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.3 (Eq. 4.6a, Example 4.3 frequency 17 MHz, Exercise 4.12)

solution_steps.explain: qB sets the angular frequency omega = qB over m

solution_steps.action: divide by 2 pi times the mass
solution_steps.explain: the ordinary frequency is qB over 2 pi m

concepts.title: Helical Path and Its Pitch
concepts.definition: If the velocity keeps a component along the field, that component rides the particle forward while the transverse part circles, producing a helix; the pitch is the forward distance covered during one turn.
concepts.key_idea: Parallel motion is untouched by the field, so the helix pitch is simply the rotation period times the axial speed.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.3 (Eq. 4.6b, pitch p = 2 pi m v_parallel / qB)
question_patterns: what is the pitch of the helix traced by a charge with velocity components across and along the field

solution_steps.explain: the transverse speed sets the helix radius r = m v_perp over qB
the time per revolution is the circumference over the transverse speed
during one turn the axial component carries the particle a distance p = v_parallel T

concepts.title: Biot-Savart Field of a Current Element
concepts.definition: Each tiny piece dl of a circuit adds a field slice dB of size (mu0 over 4 pi) I dl sin(theta) over r squared, aimed perpendicular to the plane holding the element and the line to the point; integrating the slices gives the whole field.
concepts.formula: element_field = prefactor * current * element_len * sin_tilt / distance ** 2
concepts.key_idea: Like Coulomb's law it falls off as r squared and superposes, but its source is a vector Idl and the field points crosswise, dying to zero along the element's own direction.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.4 (Eqs. 4.7a-4.7c, Example 4.4 element on the y-axis)
question_patterns: state the Biot-Savart law for the field of a small current element

solution_steps.action: build the mu0 over 4 pi prefactor
solution_steps.explain: the constant equals 1e-7 T m/A in SI units
dB = prefactor times I dl sin(theta) over r squared
solution_steps.compute: element_field = prefactor * current * element_len * sin_tilt / distance ** 2

concepts.title: Field at the Centre of a Circular Coil
concepts.definition: Adding the Biot-Savart slices around a circular loop of radius R gives a centre field mu0 I over 2R, and an N-turn coil multiplies that by N because the same current loops N times.
concepts.key_idea: Every element contributes in the same direction at the centre, so the whole circumference sums cleanly; more turns stack the field linearly.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.5 (Eq. 4.12, Examples 4.5-4.6, semicircular arc half-value)
question_patterns: find the magnetic field at the centre of a 100-turn coil of radius 8 cm carrying 0.4 A

determine the centre field when the coil current or radius changes
calculate mu0 N I over 2R for given turns, current and radius

solution_steps.action: multiply mu0 by turns and current
solution_steps.explain: N turns each contribute as if carrying the full current
the centre result is mu0 N I over 2R

concepts.title: Axial Field of a Circular Current Loop
concepts.definition: Along the symmetry axis a distance x from the loop centre, only the axial components of the element fields survive because the sideways parts cancel in pairs, leaving B = mu0 I R squared over 2 (x squared plus R squared) to the power 3/2.
concepts.key_idea: At the centre x = 0 this collapses to mu0 I over 2R, and far away it fades like 1 over x cubed.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.5 (Eqs. 4.9-4.11, cancellation of perpendicular components)
question_patterns: derive the field at a point on the axis of a circular current loop

solution_steps.explain: the slant distance r = sqrt(x squared plus R squared) enters cubed
B = mu0 I R squared over 2 times that denominator

concepts.title: Ampere's Circuital Law
concepts.definition: Around any closed loop that bounds a surface pierced by current, adding up B dot dl segment by segment gives mu0 times the enclosed current; with the right-hand sign convention the curled fingers set the positive current sense.
concepts.key_idea: The law always holds, but it solves for B by hand only when symmetry makes B constant along part of the loop and zero or sideways elsewhere, reducing it to B L = mu0 Ie.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.6 (Eqs. 4.13a-4.13b, comparison with Gauss law)

solution_steps.explain: the boundary should have B tangential and constant on some parts, normal or zero on the rest
only the tangential-constant stretch contributes, giving B times its length

solution_steps.action: equate to mu0 times enclosed current
solution_steps.explain: BL = mu0 Ie then solves for the field magnitude

concepts.title: Field of a Long Straight Current
concepts.definition: A circular amperian loop around an infinitely long wire has constant tangential B, so the field at distance r outside is mu0 I over 2 pi r, circling the wire; inside a thick wire of radius a it grows linearly as mu0 I r over 2 pi a squared.
concepts.key_idea: The field lines are closed circles around the wire, magnitude set only by r, and the right-hand grip rule gives the sense.
question_patterns: find the magnetic field 20 cm from a long wire carrying 35 A

solution_steps.explain: Ampere's law on a circle gives B 2 pi r = mu0 I

solution_steps.action: divide by the circle circumference factor
solution_steps.explain: so B = mu0 I over 2 pi r outside the wire

concepts.title: Field Inside a Long Solenoid
concepts.definition: Inside a solenoid much longer than its radius the field is nearly uniform and axial; a rectangular amperian loop threading n turns per unit length gives B = mu0 n I, while the outside field is taken as negligible.
concepts.key_idea: Turn density, not total turns, controls the field: B = mu0 n I with n = total turns over length.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.7 (Eq. 4.16, Example 4.8 solenoid field 6.28e-3 T)
question_patterns: find the field inside a 0.5 m solenoid of 500 turns carrying 5 A

solution_steps.explain: n is the total turns divided by the solenoid length
the interior field is mu0 n I

concepts.title: Force Between Parallel Currents
concepts.definition: Two long parallel conductors a distance d apart exchange a force per unit length mu0 Ia Ib over 2 pi d: same-direction currents attract, opposite ones repel, and this relation fixes the SI ampere via the 2e-7 N/m benchmark.
concepts.formula: force_per_len = mu0 * current_a * current_b / (2 * pi * separation)
concepts.key_idea: One wire's field pushes the other through the Il x B force; mutual forces stay equal and opposite, and attraction for like currents is the reverse of charges.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.8 (Eqs. 4.17-4.19, ampere definition, Example 4.9, Exercise 4.7)

solution_steps.explain: the coupling is proportional to the product Ia Ib

solution_steps.action: scale by mu0 over the geometry
solution_steps.explain: f over L equals mu0 Ia Ib divided by 2 pi d
multiply the per-length force by the segment length

concepts.title: Magnetic Moment of a Current Loop
concepts.definition: A planar loop of N turns carrying I over area A behaves like a magnetic dipole with moment m = N I A, directed by the right-hand thumb along the area vector; its units are ampere metre squared.
concepts.key_idea: Far from the loop the field matches that of a dipole of moment m, with no magnetic monopole analogue of the electric case.
question_patterns: find the magnetic moment of a 100-turn coil of radius 10 cm carrying 3.2 A

solution_steps.explain: a square of side s has area s squared; a circle uses pi R squared
m = N I A is the dipole moment of the loop

concepts.title: Torque on a Loop in a Uniform Field
concepts.definition: A current loop in a uniform field feels zero net force but a torque tau = m B sin(theta), turning the moment toward the field; parallel alignment is stable, antiparallel unstable.
concepts.key_idea: The two side arms form a couple whose lever arm shrinks with the tilt angle, so equilibrium sits where m lines up with B.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.9.1 (Eqs. 4.20-4.23, Example 4.10 parts c-d, Exercise 4.9)
question_patterns: find the torque on a suspended square coil whose normal makes 30 degrees with a 0.8 T field

solution_steps.explain: m = N I A combines turns, current and loop area
torque magnitude is m B sin(theta) with theta between m and B

concepts.title: Moving Coil Galvanometer Deflection
concepts.definition: In a radial field the coil's magnetic torque NIAB meets the spring's restoring torque k phi, so the steady deflection is proportional to current: phi = NAB I over k; the ratio NAB over k is the current sensitivity.
concepts.formula: deflection = turns * area * mag_field * current / spring_const
concepts.key_idea: Radial field keeps sin(theta) at one for every orientation, making the scale linear in current.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.10 (Eqs. 4.26-4.27, current vs voltage sensitivity)
question_patterns: derive the deflection relation phi = NAB I over k for a galvanometer

solution_steps.explain: the radial field gives full-strength torque NIAB
setting k phi equal to NIAB yields the deflection

concepts.title: Converting a Galvanometer to Ammeter or Voltmeter
concepts.definition: A tiny shunt in parallel turns the sensitive galvanometer into an ammeter by bypassing most of the current, while a large resistance in series makes it a voltmeter that draws almost none; ideal meters disturb the circuit as little as possible.
concepts.key_idea: Ammeters go in series and must add negligible resistance; voltmeters go in parallel and must draw negligible current.
concepts.textbook_ref: leph104.txt section 4.10 (shunt and series conversions, Example 4.12 readings 0.048, 0.99, 1.00 A)
question_patterns: why is a small shunt wired in parallel to use a galvanometer as an ammeter

solution_steps.explain: the parallel pair product enters the numerator
parallel combination is product over sum, close to the shunt when it is tiny
